newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tensions rise in Serbia ahead of OSCE report.
newsitem.headline: Tensions rise in Serbia ahead of OSCE report.

text.p: Tensions rose in Serbia on Sunday as rival demonstrations were held for and against President Slobodan Milosevic ahead of an OSCE verdict on alleged election fraud.
A mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) investigating Serbia's election fraud crisis wound up its work in Belgrade on Saturday.
Mission head Felipe Gonzalez, the former Spanish prime minister, has said he will make recommendations within a week.

The Zajedno coalition of opposition parties says it has proved to the OSCE that it was cheated of victory in Belgrade and 14 other towns in local elections -- the spark for huge street demonstrations against Milosevic.

Opposition sources said the OSCE persuaded Milosevic to surrender the towns, including Belgrade, but that he would exercise his right to call a fresh poll early in 1997 to try to recover them for his ruling socialists.
Gonzalez was non-committal about the outcome of the mission sent to dig Serbia out of five weeks of street demonstrations that show no sign of diminishing.
But an American member of the OSCE team, veteran diplomat Max Kampelman, said the evidence it found of election fraud "seems to be impressive."
More than 100,000 opposition supporters and students demonstrated in Belgrade on Saturday along with 40,000 in Kragujevac and 20,000 in Leskovac.
Police kept the Kragujevac protest and a socialist counter demonstration apart as the two sides traded insults.
Zajedno said the socialists were planning to hold "final" demonstrations in Belgrade in support of Milosevic on Tuesday.
It said some 1,000 buses and trains will be used to transport Milosevic supporters into the capital. The authorities were paying for the fuel and daily allowances for their supporters, Zajedno said.
Diplomats fear mounting hatred and the proximity of the two rival groups could easily spark violence both Zajedno leaders and Milosevic have promised to avoid.

The state-run media, run by socialist hardliners reported to be increasingly independent from Milosevic, has increased its campaign against the opposition, calling them traitors to the Serbian cause and servants of the West.

Zajedno accuse police of intimidating the population of smaller towns to stop them demonstrating after Vranje activist Goran Krstic was arrested and beaten on Thursday. Other arrests were reported in Zajecar and Kraljevo.

The socialists' use of courts to overturn Zajedno results for secret "irregularities" has inspired a U.S.-led push for democratic reforms in Serbia after half a century of communist and socialist rule.
Zoran Djindjic, the main Zajedno leader and its mayoral candidate in Belgrade, said:

"The differences between the original results and the unprecedented court interventions are clear to all OSCE commission members. The only question is how to reinstate the original election results and resolve the crisis."
